newsitem.title: UK: Irish election forms part of quest for peace.
newsitem.headline: Irish election forms part of quest for peace.

text.p: Irish elections on Friday will slot a new Dublin government into a jigsaw that Britain and Ireland hope can be shaped into a firm Northern Ireland peace.
Tattered truces by Republican and Loyalist guerrillas and fears of a "long hot summer" of Protestant parades and Catholic protests hover over the divided province.
After nearly three years, an Anglo-Irish peace initiative has been stalled by guerrilla conflict but politicians in both capitals say they will press ahead with the peace quest.

A New Irish government will join the new Labour administration of British Prime Minister Tony Blair in trying to reconcile the province's pro-Irish Catholic nationalists and pro-British Protestant Unionists in a political settlement.
Plans for a fresh start for the province exploded in February 1996 when IRA guerrillas broke a 17 month truce and killed two civilians in a huge blast in London.
Since then British and Irish leaders, supported by the U.S, have gingerly sought a solution.
They say it lies with the Irish Republican Army (IRA), a guerrilla force that spurns calls to reinstate a shattered ceasefire that would edge its Sinn Fein political arm into negotiations.
British Prime Minister Blair says he will not wait for ever for a new IRA truce before pressing on with political strategies to reconcile the two communities.

"My message to Sinn Fein is clear. The settlement train is leaving. I want you on that train. But it is leaving anyway, and I will not allow it to wait for you. You cannot hold the process to ransom any longer," he said in Belfast on May 16.
Political analysts say a new team could be at the helm in Dublin in 48 hours to face the challenge of helping rebuild peace.
For months torpor enveloped the peace drive before a British election in May swept out the Conservatives and installed Blair after a landslide win.
Irish nationalists had accused Conservative Prime Minister John Major of being paralysed by a need for the parliamentary support of the province's pro-British Protestant legislators.
Coasting to victory, Blair soon jetted into the region to assure all sides their problems were his problems, and that Labour was treating them as a priority.
Dublin and Washington saw Blair's emphatic victory as opening the way for fresh progress on ending Northern Ireland's impasse.
But the other half of the political equation, Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, added a further element of uncertainty to the peace drive by also opting for a poll seven months early.

Northern Ireland surfaced briefly but belligerently in the campaign. Bruton's main opponent Fianna Fail, led by Bertie Ahern and well ahead in the polls, regards itself as the true descendent of patriots who won freedom from Britain in 1922.

Labour Party leader Dick Spring, deputy to Bruton in a three-party alliance, attended Northern Ireland multi-party talks in Belfast last week but parties there wondered whether a new face might take his place at next week's session.

Britain's election changed the political landscape of Northern Ireland. Sinn Fein dramatically strengthened its support among minority Catholics by capturing two parliamentary seats, its best performance for 40 years.

Old fault lines have deepended however and the jigsaw is getting harder to piece together. In comfortable suburbs, people remain apprehensive. In town centres sectarian hatred erupts in mobs kicking a defenceless Catholic or Protestant into pulp.
Two people, including a policeman, have been kicked to death in the past few weeks, and at least one other narrowly survived.
IRA activists are sabre-rattling after a short lull led to talks between Sinn Fein and British officials.
Britain insists on a formal end to violence as Sinn Fein's ticket to talks. Republicans say they need a firm date for a talks seat to woo the IRA to call a fresh cessation.
Pro-British Loyalist guerrillas, whose October 1994 truce has been breached several times though never formally abandoned, remain a severe threat.
On the streets a Protestant "marching season" that last year brought the province to the brink of anarchy is getting into swing, with no sign of Catholic objectors being mollified.
They say the yearly parades are intimidation and want them rerouted but there are scant signs of compromise with the main marches in July only weeks away.
